title: How the scheduler decides who runs next
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain what the scheduler is optimising for, predict the effect of a nice value with real numbers, and say why a CPU-bound and an I/O-bound program get treated differently.

blocks.text: There are almost always more runnable threads than cores. The scheduler decides who gets a core and for how long, thousands of times a second, and it has to satisfy two goals that pull against each other: keep the cores busy, and keep interactive things feeling instant.

rows: Runs briefly, then blocks on a read
A shell, an editor, a web server
Latency — to be run soon after it wakes
Leaves the core free most of the time

blocks.text: Linux's normal scheduler favours whichever thread has received the least CPU time relative to its weight. A thread that keeps blocking on I/O accumulates very little run time, so when it wakes it is near the front of the queue — which is exactly why your shell stays responsive during a compile. The interactive behaviour falls out of the fairness rule; it is not a special case.

A nice value from -20 to 19 changes a thread's weight in that calculation. Higher nice means lower priority — it is 'how nice you are being to others'. Only privileged processes may set a negative value.

headers: Setup (two CPU hogs pinned to one core, 3 seconds each)

blocks.title: Where those ratios come from
blocks.text: Each step of nice multiplies a thread's weight by roughly 1.25. Ten steps is about 1.25^10, near 9.3; nineteen steps is about 1.25^19, near 69 — and the kernel's own weight table puts nice 0 against nice 19 at 1024/15, about 68. The measured ratios of 10.6 and 75 land close to those predictions. This is worth knowing because it means nice is not a mild hint: at nice 19 a background job gets a couple of percent of a contended core.

blocks.title: Measure contention, or you measure nothing
blocks.text: The first version of this experiment ran in a container limited with a CPU quota rather than pinned to a specific core, and the results were meaningless — the nice 19 process sometimes did MORE work, because both processes simply ran on different cores and never competed. Priority only expresses itself when threads are actually contending for the same core. Pin to one core (taskset -c 0, or the container's cpuset option) before drawing any conclusion.

rows: Everything normal; fair sharing by weight
Real-time: runs until it blocks or yields
Real-time with a time slice between equals
Only when nothing else wants the core

blocks.title: A real-time policy can hang the machine
blocks.text: A SCHED_FIFO thread runs until it blocks. A busy loop at that policy will not be preempted by ordinary work, including the shell you would use to kill it. Verified on one machine: the real-time priority range is 1 to 99, while SCHED_OTHER reports a range of 0 to 0 because it uses nice instead. Real-time policies belong to audio, robotics and instrumentation — not to 'this service feels slow'.
What actually causes a slow system

items: Runnable threads far exceeding cores — check the load average against the core count
Threads blocked on I/O, which no priority change will speed up
Lock contention, which looks like poor CPU use rather than high CPU use
One process at a very high nice value being starved by everything else

blocks.text: Adjusting priorities is the last of those to reach for, not the first. If the load average is well under the core count and things still feel slow, the problem is waiting, not scheduling — and the earlier lessons in this module cover what it is waiting on.

blocks.title: Measure priority, correctly
steps: Write a program that loops doing arithmetic for exactly 3 seconds and prints how many iterations it completed
Run two copies at the same time on an unloaded machine — they should complete similar amounts
Now pin both to one core: taskset -c 0 ./hog & taskset -c 0 ./hog & wait
Confirm they now split that core roughly evenly
Run: taskset -c 0 ./hog & taskset -c 0 nice -n 10 ./hog & wait     and compare
Repeat with nice -n 19 and work out the ratio
Run: uptime and compare the load average with nproc
Read: cat /proc/self/sched | head -12    (the accounting the scheduler keeps for you)
blocks.expected: Near-equal shares at equal nice, roughly ten-to-one at nice 10, and roughly seventy-to-one at nice 19. If you skip the pinning step, you will get noise — which is the most useful mistake in this lesson to make once, deliberately.

cheatsheet: The scheduler balances throughput against interactive latency
Linux favours the thread with the least run time relative to its weight
I/O-bound threads accumulate little run time, so they wake up near the front — responsiveness follows from fairness
nice runs -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest); negative values need privilege
Measured on one contended core: nice 0 vs 10 is about 10.6x; nice 0 vs 19 is about 75x
Each nice step is roughly a 1.25x weight change
Priority only matters under contention — pin to one core before measuring
SCHED_FIFO/RR are real-time, priority 1-99, and a busy loop there can lock up the machine
Slow system: compare load average with nproc; suspect I/O and locks before priority

checkpoint.prompt: Why does your shell stay responsive during a long compile, without any special configuration?

choices.A: Shells are given a real-time priority
choices.B: The compiler yields the CPU voluntarily
choices.C: The kernel detects interactive programs by name

checkpoint.explanation: It accumulates almost no run time and is near the front of the queue whenever it wakes. Interactive responsiveness falls out of the fairness rule rather than being a special case: whoever has used the least gets picked first.

checkpoint.prompt: Two CPU-bound processes share one core, one at nice 0 and one at nice 19. Roughly what share does the nice 19 process get?

choices.A: None at all — it is never scheduled

checkpoint.explanation: Measured at roughly 75 to 1. Each nice step is about a 1.25x weight change, so nineteen steps is roughly 1.25^19, near 69 — the kernel's weight table itself puts nice 0 against nice 19 at 1024/15, about 68. It still runs; it just gets very little.

checkpoint.prompt: You compare nice 0 with nice 19 on an idle 10-core machine and see no difference. Why?

choices.A: You need root to use nice
choices.B: nice does not work on modern kernels
choices.D: With free cores there is no contention

checkpoint.explanation: Both simply run — priority only expresses itself when threads compete for the same core. This exact mistake produced meaningless numbers when this lesson's measurements were first taken. Pin both to one core, then measure.

checkpoint.prompt: A service feels slow. Load average is 0.4 on an 8-core machine. What is the likely cause?

choices.A: It needs a better nice value
choices.B: It is waiting — on I/O or on a lock
choices.C: Too few cores for the volume of requests
choices.D: The scheduler policy is set wrong for this service

checkpoint.explanation: A load average far below the core count means there is plenty of idle CPU, so the CPU is not the constraint. Changing priority cannot speed up something that is not running because it is blocked.
